## Decision
Do not invest this money. First check your overdraft terms today. Then repay any part of the £4,000 that is already charged interest, or will be within about 12 months. If the whole overdraft is still free for over a year, hold that cash in easy-access savings and clear the overdraft a month before the free period ends.

## Why
- Overdrafts above the free limit often cost about 39% to 40% EAR. At 39%, £4,000 costs about £1,560 a year, or £130 a month. No investment reliably beats that.
- Shares can fall 20% or more in a year. You owe a debt with a deadline. Money needed within 5 years does not belong in shares.
- Some banks shrink the free limit each year. NatWest, for example, steps down from £3,250 to £2,250 to £1,250. So only part of your £4,000 may be at risk of interest soon.
- If the debt is free, savings at about 4.5% would earn roughly £180 a year on £4,000. That is about £15 a month. It is a small gain, so do not take risks for it.

## Main risks
- Missing the date when the free period ends. Cost then jumps to about £130 a month.
- Banks can cut or withdraw an overdraft limit, and it is repayable on demand.
- Paying off everything leaves £1,000. That is under one month of cover for most people. You may drift back into the overdraft.
- Savings rates quoted online may include short bonuses. Check them yourself. I could not verify the figures.
- A Lifetime ISA has a 25% withdrawal charge. On a bad exit you lose about 6.25% of your own money. Rules were under review, so check gov.uk.

## Honest criticism for the owner
- You asked a question that depends on a number you have not looked up. Your rate and your free-period end date decide this. Everything else is guesswork.
- You are treating this £5,000 as the big decision. At 24, your monthly habit matters more. A steady monthly investment over decades will beat this one choice.
- Having no emergency fund beyond this £5,000 is a weakness. Do not leave yourself with nothing.
- Clearing the overdraft does not close it. Do not spend back into it.

## Next steps
1. Today, in your banking app: write down your rate, your free-period end date and your yearly limit steps. Set a calendar alert one month before the free period ends.
2. By 1 November 2026: repay the part that will be charged interest within 12 months. Keep the rest in easy-access savings. Aim for 3 months of spending as a buffer, and build it from monthly pay.
3. Once the overdraft is clear: take any employer pension match from salary. Then start a monthly low-cost global fund, only with money you can leave for 5+ years.

## Board notes
- I overruled the Advocate and the Operator on the pension match and Lifetime ISA. Pension contributions come from salary, not from this £5,000, so they do not compete for this cash.
- I partly overruled the 39% figure applied to the full £4,000. It only applies to the amount above your free limit.
- Open: the Operator's £200 a month saving is an assumption. We have no income or spending data.

## Decision
Launch in October, by Oct 31, as a soft launch in one narrow niche. Do not wait for January. Treat October to December as a cheap test, and set a stop-or-continue date of Jan 31.

## Why
- Launching costs about $0.20 per listing plus your time. Waiting saves almost nothing and gains no proven benefit.
- You get about 10 weeks of views, favorites, and search data before January. Reviews help conversion, so early ones are worth having.
- The board found no Notion-specific data showing January beats other months. Seller blogs put the back-to-school peak between June and August, and they disagree. A January bump is plausible but unconfirmed.
- Fees are modest without ads: about 6.5% plus 3% plus $0.25 per sale, plus $0.20 per listing. A $12 sale nets about $10.40. Confirm on etsy.com/legal/fees.

## Main risks
- **No differentiation.** Notion student planners are a crowded category. A generic planner will not sell at any date.
- **Zero traffic.** New shops often get few views at first. I have no reliable rate.
- **Review rules.** Etsy bans paying or rewarding buyers for reviews. Friend and family reviews risk a flag. Do not offer discounts in exchange for reviews.
- **Brand and content rights.** Check Notion's brand rules for your listing name and images. Check licenses on fonts, icons, and covers. Check Etsy's rules on disclosing AI use.
- **Money.** New sellers may face payout holds and a setup fee of about $15. If your annual sales pass $10,000, Offsite Ads become mandatory and take 12% to 15% of attributed sales.
- **Link sharing.** Anyone with the duplicate link can pass it on. Notion can also change template features.
- **Free competition.** Many free Notion templates exist, and that caps your price.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You did not tell us what makes your planner different. That matters more than the month. You also did not give your weekly hours, your budget, or your price. Expect $0 to $100 by mid-January. A realistic year-one range is a few hundred dollars, perhaps up to $2,000 with several listings. These are estimates, not data. Finishing the build was the easy part. Winning attention is the hard part.

## Next steps
1. By Oct 22: do a 30-minute check. Search Etsy for your niche and note the top 10 listings' prices and review counts. Check Google Trends for "notion planner" over 5 years. If you cannot name one clear difference, fix that first.
2. By Oct 31: open the shop and publish with 5 or more images and a short video. Price at $10 to $15. Test the duplicate link on a second account and confirm your free-plan compatibility. Start identity and bank setup now, since it can take days.
3. Check stats on Nov 28 (under 100 views means rewrite the title and main image). Refresh by Dec 15 by editing the same listing, not relisting. Decide on Jan 31 whether to continue or stop.

## Board notes
- I overruled the claim that new listings are buried by ranking. Etsy does not say this. The case for October rests on cost and learning time.
- I overruled the "January relaunch test." It changes season and photos together, so it proves little.
- Open: whether a lower launch price ($8 to $10) beats $12 or more for early sales. No one checked live prices.

## Decision
Do not sell yet, and do not commit to keeping it either. Spend the next four to six weeks getting your real figures. Sell only if your yield after tax is below about 4% (or below what your sale money could safely earn elsewhere), or if a major works bill is pending. Otherwise keep it and fight the charge.

## Why
- Nobody can call this without your numbers. Two sharp rises usually have a cause: insurance, a new managing agent, or repair backlog. The cause decides everything.
- Rent will not rescue you. The ONS average for a Manchester one-bed is about £993 a month (June 2026). A £50 a month charge rise is about 5% of that.
- Selling is costly and slower than it looks. Agent and legal fees may run 1.5% to 3% of the price. Capital gains tax is 18% or 24% above a £3,000 allowance.
- Section 21 no-fault eviction reportedly ended on 1 May 2026. I have not seen GOV.UK confirm this. Selling with a tenant in place is now harder. Selling to another landlord with the tenant in place may be the easiest route. That is an inference, not a verified fact.

## Main risks
- **Section 20 works bill.** Works over £250 per flat need consultation. A bill could be thousands of pounds.
- **Cladding or fire safety costs.** The Building Safety Act may protect some leaseholders. I am unsure whether you qualify.
- **Mortgage reset.** If your fix ends soon, the flat may go cash negative.
- **Weaker resale.** Buyers and lenders look hard at high service charges. Waiting could lower your price.
- **Disclosure.** If you sell, you must answer buyers' solicitors honestly about known works. Hiding a notice risks a collapsed sale or a misrepresentation claim.
- **Rent rises.** The tenant can challenge them at tribunal, so a reset to market is not guaranteed.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You asked sell or keep without giving a single figure. That is a guess, not a decision. You also seem to treat the charge as fixed. It may be challengeable at the First-tier Tribunal under section 27A, but outcomes are mixed. Do not count on a win. Also, you did not say if the flat is let now or when the tenancy began. That date strongly affects how you can sell.

## Next steps
1. **By 25 Oct:** Gather rent, 3 years of service charge, ground rent, mortgage balance, rate, fix end date and early repayment charge, and purchase price.
2. **By 1 Nov:** Email the managing agent in writing for 3 years of accounts, budget, reserve fund balance and any planned or notified major works.
3. **By 15 Nov:** Get two agent sale valuations, one rent valuation, and a capital gains tax estimate from an accountant. Then compare after-tax yield with what the net sale money would earn. Decide by end of November.

## Board notes
- I overruled the Skeptic's "sell before buyers see it". It is risky and may be unlawful in effect.
- I did not adopt the 4% threshold as fact. Operator and Skeptic gave it without a source. Treat it as a rough guide against current cash rates, which nobody checked.
- Still open: the Ground 1A sale rules differ between sources. Check GOV.UK or a solicitor before planning a vacant sale.

## Decision
Skip the Google Data Analytics certificate. Learn Python, but only after a 1-week check of your own SQL level and your team's tools. Use a real work task as the project, and aim to finish it by 11 January 2027.

## Why
- You already have the job. The certificate is built for people seeking a first role, and it covers spreadsheets, SQL, Tableau and R. Most detailed reviews say it does not teach Python. I could not confirm this on Google's own page.
- The certificate costs about 240 to 260 hours (6 months at 10 hours a week) and roughly $300 at about $49 a month. These are recalled figures, so check Coursera.
- Python is free to learn. A real work task makes it stick far better than course exercises.
- Job posting surveys put SQL ahead of Python (SQL about 53% to 90%, Python about 31% to 55%). The surveys are rough and disagree. So if your SQL is weak, fix that first.

## Main risks
- **Learning without a use.** If you cannot name one task to automate within 30 days, you will likely forget Python.
- **Company rules.** Check that you may run scripts, export data and install software. Do not move sensitive or personal data to personal machines or public GitHub. That is a legal and job risk.
- **Silent errors.** An automated report with a bug can reach management. Run it beside the manual version for 2 to 3 cycles.
- **Time slippage.** Work crunch can cost 2 to 3 weeks. Plan for that.
- **Money.** Low. Kaggle and pandas docs are free. Coursera is the only real spend, and you can avoid it.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You asked "which course," but you did not say what you want. Promotion, a new job and a move toward data science need different skills. You also gave no SQL level, no team tools and no weekly hours. Without those, no timeline can be trusted. Choosing a credential is also an easy way to feel productive without changing your work. A finished project at your job counts for more.

## Next steps
1. This week, spend 1 hour: rate your SQL, ask your manager what tools the team uses and whether Python is allowed, and read 5 postings for the role you want next. If SQL is weak or Python is not wanted, do SQL first.
2. Block 3 sessions of 2 hours a week from Monday 19 October 2026. Use Kaggle Learn's free Python and Pandas courses, then your own work data (with permission).
3. Pick one recurring report to automate. Checkpoint on 11 January 2027: one finished, checked project. If not done, find out why before spending any money.

## Board notes
- I overruled the claim that Python speeds the path to mid-level roles, and the claim that 72 hours leads to mid-level applications. Neither has evidence. A finished project does more than hours studied.
- Open: Advanced Data Analytics certificate. One member says it is longer and costlier than the basic one, another recalls it as similar. It covers Python, but I could not verify its length or price.
- Open: whether the Google certificate teaches any Python. Check the current syllabus.

## Decision
Pay exactly 5% into the pension to get the full match. Put your next deposit money into a Lifetime ISA (LISA), up to £4,000 a year, if you are under 40, a first-time buyer, and the home costs £450,000 or less. Do not pay more than 5% into the pension while the deposit is the goal, unless you pay 40% tax and your deposit is already covered.

## Why
- The match is an instant return on your own contribution. Nothing else beats it. This assumes the employer matches pound for pound. I do not know your scheme.
- Pension money is locked until age 55, rising to 57 from 6 April 2028. You cannot use it for a deposit.
- A LISA gives a 25% bonus, up to £1,000 a year. That equals basic-rate pension relief, but you can reach it for a first home.
- Extra pension only wins clearly at higher rates. At 40% tax, £1,000 in the pension costs about £600. Between £100,000 and £125,140 income, the effective relief is about 60%.

## Main risks
- **LISA 12-month rule.** An account opened today qualifies in October 2027. Buying sooner means you cannot use it.
- **LISA penalty.** Withdrawing for anything else costs 25%. On £5,000 you get £3,750, which is £250 less than you paid in. A failed purchase triggers this.
- **Price cap.** A home over £450,000 rules out the LISA. This is common in London and the South East.
- **Reform.** The LISA may change. I found no final rules, so check gov.uk.
- **No cash cushion.** Locked money plus no emergency fund can force you into debt.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You gave us no age, salary, tax band, target price, purchase date, or monthly surplus. Those decide the answer. Without them, this is a default plan, not a tailored one. You may also be assuming "match up to 5%" means doubling your money. Check your scheme rules and ask HR whether the match rises if you pay more. That could change this advice.

## Next steps
1. This week: check your payslip shows at least 5%. Ask HR about the match rules and salary sacrifice.
2. This month: open a LISA if eligible, since the 12-month clock starts at opening. Keep about 3 months of spending in easy-access cash.
3. Then pay about £333 a month into the LISA (£4,000 a year, £5,000 with bonus). Review in April 2027, when the new tax year starts.

## Board notes
- Overruled Scout's "don't pay extra into your pension" as too absolute. It does not hold for higher-rate or £100,000 to £125,140 earners.
- Overruled Operator's "£500 a month" example. The £4,000 cap means £333 a month. Operator's "cash first" order stands, but 3 months of cash is common advice, not a rule.
- Open: whether the LISA bonus will change to payment only at purchase. One source suggested it, but it looked like a test site, so I treat it as unconfirmed.

## Decision
Do not move for the £4,000. Move only if the startup shows at least 18 months of cash runway in evidence you can check yourself, and the role gives you scope or a title you cannot get where you are within two years. If either test fails, stay.

## Why
- The raise is small. £4,000 gross is about £2,320 a year after tax and National Insurance at the 40% band, and about £2,880 at the 20% band. That is roughly £190 to £240 a month. Student loan repayments would cut it further.
- Lost benefits can erase it. A 5% employer pension match on a £40,000 salary is £2,000 a year. Bonus, health cover, sick pay and holiday days also count. Salary is unknown, so that figure is only an example.
- The downside is much larger than the upside. A 3-month gap on £2,500 a month take-home costs £7,500, which is about three years of the raise.
- Real upside exists, but it is in learning and scope, not pay. That is only worth taking if the role is clearly bigger than yours.

## Main risks
- **Job loss:** The startup may cut staff or run out of money. No reliable survival figure exists for funded startups. The 38% five-year survival figure covers all new businesses, including sole traders, so it overstates the risk.
- **Legal:** Unfair dismissal protection currently needs 2 years of service. The Employment Rights Act 2025 is reported to cut this to 6 months for dismissals from 1 January 2027. I have not verified this myself. If you move, your clock restarts. You would likely have no protection for the first months, and probation terms may allow quick dismissal.
- **Redundancy pay:** Statutory redundancy pay needs 2 years' service. Whether that is changing is unconfirmed. Check gov.uk.
- **Equity:** Treat it as worth zero until written terms prove otherwise.
- **Savings:** Moving with less than 3 to 6 months of expenses saved is unsafe.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You are focused on the number, and the number is the weakest part of the offer. You also have not said what your current job offers for growth, or what the new role actually involves. Without those, you cannot judge this. Do not assume you can return to your old employer. Asking for a counter-offer can also mark you as a leaver, so do it only if you would genuinely accept it.

## Next steps
1. **By 25 October:** Ask the startup for last funding date and amount, months of cash, and why the role is open. Check Companies House filings yourself. Do not rely on the founder's word. Also ask how long the offer stays open.
2. **By 1 November:** Get the written offer. Compare pension, bonus, notice period, probation terms, redundancy terms and any equity (share count, strike price, vesting, whether it is EMI) line by line with your current package.
3. **By 15 November:** Confirm you have 3 to 6 months of expenses saved, then decide. Walk away if runway is under 18 months or the total package is not clearly better.

## Board notes
- I set the 40% band take-home at about £2,320, not the £2,400 or £2,800 to £3,000 some members used. They left out National Insurance.
- Members disagreed on the runway floor (12 vs 18 months). I chose 18 because fundraising can take about 6 months. It is a rule of thumb, not sourced evidence.
- One member's point that employer pension contributions can be lost was overruled. UK employer contributions normally belong to you at once.

## Decision
Do not pay the £400 yet. Spend the next 14 days on free SQL material, with a hard target of 10 logged hours by 1 November 2026. Buy a course only if you miss that target, or if the course passes the checks below.

## Why
- Free content covers the same ground as most paid syllabi. SQLBolt, Kaggle Learn, SQLZoo and Mode's tutorial are well known. I have not rechecked that each is still current.
- The £400 buys structure and feedback, not extra content. A comparable listing found was £420 for 12 hours, about £35 an hour. That is a rough benchmark from one or two listings.
- Course completion figures of 60 to 96% come from vendor blogs and ignore selection bias. Do not lean on them.
- A cheap paid middle option exists. One listing showed a 20-hour self-paced course at £31 and a lifetime plan at £119. Treat those prices as unconfirmed.
- The test costs nothing and shows whether your real problem is content or follow-through.

## Main risks
- **Money:** paying £400 for a weak course with no project, no refund and the wrong SQL dialect (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server).
- **Seat risk:** the next intake may start before your test ends. Check the date.
- **Cancellation:** small evening classes can be cancelled for low enrolment. Get the terms in writing.
- **Drift:** free learning with no stop rule can fade for months. A certificate from a private course likely carries little weight, though I found no hiring data.
- **Legal:** read the refund and cancellation terms before you pay.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You have not said why you want SQL. A career move worth £3,000 a year makes £400 small. Curiosity makes it hard to justify. Without that answer, any route drifts. You also have not said how many hours a week you have, or whether you have quit self-study before. That history is the best predictor here. Finally, you have not asked your employer to fund it. That costs nothing.

## Next steps
1. Today: log hours from now. Use Kaggle Learn's Intro to SQL, then SQLBolt. Pass mark: at least 4 hours by 25 October and 10 hours by 1 November. Below 4 hours by day 7 counts as a stall.
2. This week: email the course provider for the syllabus, start dates, dialect, refund policy, cancellation terms, and whether there is reviewed project work. Also ask your employer about funding.
3. On 1 November: if you hit 10 hours, stay free and start a project on UK government open data. If you stalled, or the course passes the checks, consider the course. Try the £31 to £119 self-paced option first.

## Board notes
- I overruled the opening claim that the course is "not worth £400". It was made before anyone saw the course.
- The Operator's "£20 an hour" assumed 20 class hours that nobody confirmed. I used the £35 benchmark with caution.
- Still open: whether free learning reaches junior analyst level in 240 hours. No evidence supports that estimate.

## Decision
Post about your side projects, but only after you read your contract and confirm each project is clearly unrelated to your employer's business. Start with the projects that pass that check. Hold any project that overlaps until you have written approval or legal advice.

## Why
The post itself is rarely the danger. The danger is a clause in your contract that claims your work or requires approval. Posting is cheap and can build a visible record of your skills. The gains are slow and modest, so there is no reason to rush before the check. A dated public post cuts both ways. It can show you built something on your own time, and it can show an overlap or a missed approval.

## Main risks
- **Ownership claim.** Invention assignment clauses can claim work that relates to your employer's business, even on your own time and gear. California Labor Code 2870 limits this but excludes related work. Other places give less protection. I am unsure which rules apply to you.
- **Approval or conflict rules.** Posting without required approval can lead to a warning or dismissal.
- **Confidentiality leaks.** One careless number, tool name or client detail can be traced to you. A result you cite may come from work knowledge.
- **Legal cost.** A lawyer consult likely costs $200 to $500 per hour in the US. I am unsure of the figure for your country.
- **Money from the project.** If a project earns income, tax and moonlighting rules may apply.
- **Manager perception.** This is real but unmeasurable. The firing surveys found cover inappropriate posts, not project posts.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You asked whether it could hurt, but you did not say your country, your employer's field or what the projects are. Those three facts decide almost everything. You may also be treating "my own time, my own laptop" as enough. In many places it is not, if the work relates to your employer's business. And you are planning content before checking the contract. That order is backwards. Expect small results, perhaps a few hundred views per post. Do not expect job offers.

## Next steps
1. **By Oct 25 (1 to 2 hours, $0):** Read your offer letter and handbook. Find the invention assignment, outside activities, confidentiality and social media clauses. Note whether your profile names your employer.
2. **By Nov 1:** Sort each project into clear or overlapping. If any clause is broad or unclear, book a one-hour employment lawyer consult before you tell anyone at work. Ask HR or your manager only after that, and only if needed.
3. **From Nov 8:** Post about clear projects only, every 2 weeks, using 2 to 4 hours per post. Use no employer details and no work hours. Stop and reassess if anyone flags overlap.

## Board notes
- I overruled the claim that telling your manager first is always wise. It can trigger an approval process or a claim. Check the contract first.
- I overruled the "more likely to help than hurt" claim. No member had data for it.
- Open: no member could verify court rulings or non-compete timing. Treat the legal points as general, not advice.

9.text:
## Decision
Do not join at a flat 30% as a permanent plan. Run a short pilot of about 8 weeks only if you get a lower tier (15% to 25%) or if your own numbers show profit at 30%. Run it in quiet hours only, with higher app prices and a written quit rule.

## Why
- At 30%, you only profit on orders you would not have got anyway. Example: on a 20.00 order, you keep about 7.20 before labor. In the shop the same sale leaves about 14.
- Regulars who switch to the app cost you money. If half the orders are your regulars, the pilot likely loses about 420 a month after labor. This is an illustration, not your data.
- The all-in cost is often higher than 30%. Payment processing (2% to 4%), ads and refunds add to it. Vendor blogs say 30% to 40%. Those sources sell software, so treat them with caution.
- A price rise of 10% to 15% recovers only part of the fee. Full recovery at 30% needs about 43%, and customers will not accept that on most items.
- Quiet hours are the real upside. Your rent and staff are already paid, so extra orders then cost little.

## Main risks
- **Money:** Switching regulars, refunds for cold or spilled orders, and hidden fees.
- **Contract:** Lock-in, notice periods, price parity rules and fee changes at short notice. I have not seen your contract.
- **Local law:** Some cities cap commissions (reportedly 15% in New York City and San Francisco). I am unsure about your city. Check it.
- **Operations:** Orders during your rush slow in-store service.
- **Reputation:** Bad app reviews are public.
- **Dependence:** The app owns the customer data.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You asked about 30% as if it were fixed. It is usually the top tier, and you may be able to choose a cheaper one. You also gave no numbers. Without your food cost, average order and quiet-hour traffic, no one can say if this pays. Do not expect delivery to transform the café. A realistic gain is modest, and it depends on how many orders come from new customers. You must find a way to measure that.

## Next steps
1. This week: pull 90 days of till data (average order, food cost %, quiet hours). Get the fee tier, processing fee and contract in writing. Check for a local commission cap.
2. If the numbers work, launch by early November with 10 to 12 items that travel well, app prices 15% to 20% higher, and quiet hours only. Budget about 300 to 800 for a tablet and packaging.
3. Write your quit rule now. At day 30, stop if fewer than 40% of orders are new customers. At day 60, stop if net profit after labor, fees and refunds is under 400 a month. Avoid judging only on holiday weeks.

## Board notes
- I overruled the Operator's "half regulars" case. The correct result is about -420 a month, not +120.
- I did not adopt the Scout's "ingredient cost under 20%" rule or the Skeptic's "60% margin" bar. Neither is derived from data. Open question: whether a lowest-tier trial gets enough visibility to teach you anything.
- The members disagree on the stop figure (1.50 or 2.00 per order). I used monthly net and new-customer share instead.

## Decision
Move only if you are in the office at least 3 to 4 days a week and your net extra cost, after dropping your fares, is under about £200 a month. Check three facts first, by Sunday 25 October 2026. If any check fails, stay put and ask for remote days instead.

## Why
- £300 a month is £3,600 a year. At 5 office days a week you regain about 440 hours a year, so about £8 an hour. At 3 days it is about £13 an hour. At 2 days it is over £20.
- Your current fares or fuel are saved when you move. That could cut the real price well below £300. Nobody has your figure yet.
- Research (ONS 2014, Stutzer and Frey, Clark) links long commutes with lower wellbeing. The effects are small and observational, so they support moving only mildly.
- Your new commute will not be zero. Saving 2 hours a day is the ceiling, not the likely figure.

## Main risks
- **Office days fall.** Rent stays fixed while the benefit shrinks. This is the most likely failure.
- **One-off costs.** Expect £1,000 to £2,000 for removals, fees and overlap rent. The extra deposit (about £350) is refundable.
- **Hidden running costs.** Council tax band, bills and parking may add to the £300.
- **Tenancy terms.** In England, the Renters' Rights Act should have ended fixed terms from 1 May 2026, so you may leave on about 2 months' notice. I am fairly sure but not certain, and Scotland and Wales differ. Check your own contract.
- **Cash buffer.** If the move leaves you under 3 months of costs in savings, do not do it.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You gave no office days, fares, income or location. Those decide this, and you have not done the sums. You are also treating "time saved" as a pure gain. It only helps if you use it well. Do not assume a shorter commute will make you happier. The average studies cannot tell you that.

## Next steps
1. By 25 October: pull your monthly commute cost from bank statements, and get your office days for the next 12 months in writing.
2. By 25 October: check Rightmove or Zoopla for real rents near work, plus council tax and bills, to find the true monthly gap.
3. Before signing: confirm notice period, deposit and fees. Sign only if rent is affordable (a common guide is under about 35% of take-home pay) and you keep 3 months of savings. Aim for a January move, not December.

## Board notes
- I overruled the claim that a 12-month lock-in is certain. Scout's point on the Renters' Rights Act is likely right for England, but it is unverified here.
- I treated the "4 days" cut-off and the 35% rent rule as rules of thumb, not facts. I used a looser 3 to 4 days.
- Open: the ONS commute bands may refer to one-way time, which would put you at the edge of the worst band, not in it. Not confirmed.

## Decision
Buy the used car, but only if paying £6,000 still leaves you at least 3 months of living costs in savings, plus £1,000 set aside for repairs. If it does not, do not lease by default. Look at a cheaper car or a smaller purchase first.

## Why
- Over 3 years, buying looks cheaper. Lease: about £9,750 to £11,000 once the upfront payment is counted, and you own nothing. Buy: roughly £3,500 to £6,500 after resale and repairs. The gap is probably £3,000 to £6,000.
- A lease has no mileage cap problem if you buy. You also avoid hand-back damage bills and early exit fees, which can be most of the remaining payments.
- You can keep the car past 3 years. A lease restarts the payments.
- Lost interest on £6,000 at about 4% is £240 a year, or £720 over 3 years. That narrows the gap but does not close it.

## Main risks
- Repairs. £6,000 usually buys a car 7 to 10 years old in the UK. One failure (clutch, gearbox) can cost £800 to £2,000.
- Buying a dud: hidden finance, clocked mileage, accident history. A legal risk too, as you could lose a car with outstanding finance.
- Draining your emergency cash. I do not know your savings.
- Financing the purchase. A loan at 8% to 10% APR would cut the gap sharply.
- Lease: credit check, lock-in, excess mileage (about 6p to 15p a mile), and damage charges.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You compared £6,000 with £250 a month. That is not a fair comparison. You gave us no mileage, savings, car or lease quote, so every figure here is an estimate, and the resale values are guesses nobody checked against a real listing. The lease headline also hides the upfront payment. Do not decide on the monthly price alone.

## Next steps
1. This week: confirm that £6,000 is spare cash and that you keep 3 months of costs. Work out your yearly mileage.
2. Within 7 days: get 3 written lease quotes showing the total of all payments, the mileage cap and the excess rate. Also check Auto Trader for 3 real £6,000 cars and get insurance quotes for them.
3. Within 3 weeks: buy only a car with a full service history, an HPI check (about £20) and an independent inspection (£100 to £200).

## Board notes
- I overruled the claim that a £6,000 car is 3 to 5 years old. That is unlikely in the UK, so resale of £3,800 to £4,500 is optimistic. I plan on about £3,500.
- I overruled the claim that older cars are cheaper to insure. It depends on your age and postcode.
- Still open: the true size of the gap. Nobody checked a real car or a real lease quote.

## Decision
Do not agree to a plain 50/50 handshake. Agree to explore the partnership, and say yes only after a written agreement with vesting, defined roles, a deadlock rule and a buyout clause. Reply to your friend by November 1, 2026, after a short customer test.

## Why
- An even split is common, so the split is not the main problem. Missing paperwork is. Without it, a partner who quits in month 3 could keep 50% for good.
- Deadlock has no tiebreaker at 50/50. Courts are a poor fix. Dissolution is discretionary and slow, and I am unsure how your state or country handles it.
- Asking for terms in writing costs almost nothing. A good partner welcomes it. A partner who dodges it has told you something.
- The upside depends on what your friend brings. A skill, customers or capital you lack makes this worth doing. Enthusiasm alone does not.

## Main risks
- **Money:** You could lose everything you put in. Only invest what you can lose and still pay your bills. Setup costs are unknown. Estimates range from about USD 1,000 to 10,000 in year one, and none is sourced.
- **Legal:** Without an LLC or similar entity, you may be personally liable for business debts and your partner's acts. Rules vary by place. I am not a lawyer.
- **Ownership:** If you work together before signing, who owns that work is unclear.
- **Employer:** Your job contract may give your employer a claim on what you build.
- **Tax:** In the US, vesting stock may need an 83(b) election within 30 days. LLCs differ. Ask an accountant.
- **Friendship:** A money fight can end both the business and the friendship.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You asked "should I agree?" without telling us the business, the money, the hours or your friend's actual offer. That is a warning sign. You may be reacting to the flattery of being asked. Also, trust built socially does not show how your friend acts when money is lost. Do not assume it does. Ask yourself why the offer is 50/50. If the answer is "it feels fair," that is not a reason.

## Next steps
1. **By October 25:** Both write down hours per week, cash in, roles, and a one-sentence offer (what you sell, to whom, why they pay). Check your employer contract. Sign a one-page note on who owns work done before the deal.
2. **By November 1:** Talk to 10 potential customers (about USD 0 to 100). Ask your friend to accept 4-year vesting with a 1-year cliff, a tiebreaker such as mediation then arbitration, and a buy-sell clause. Treat 10 chats as weak evidence, since people are polite.
3. **Before any money goes in:** Pay a lawyer to draft the agreement and form the entity. Budget roughly USD 1,500 to 5,000, which is a guess. Set a stop rule: no paying customer by day 90 means you close or reassess.

## Board notes
- I overruled the Advocate on 51/49 being weak and the Skeptic on it being a fix. Neither is proven. Named decision owners per area plus a tiebreaker are the better tools.
- I overruled Scout's "say no for now" as stricter than the evidence. "Not yet, pending terms" is the fair reading.
- Open: the board gave conflicting cost and revenue figures, all unsourced. Treat them as placeholders.

## Decision
Do not move your investments out of index funds. Keep at least 90% in broad index funds. If you still want to pick stocks, use a small side portion of 5% of your money, funded with new savings, and judge it over 5 years.

## Why
- Most professionals lose to the index. S&P's SPIVA report for year-end 2024 found no US active fund category with a majority beating its benchmark over 15 years. An amateur has no obvious reason to do better.
- A few stocks drive the gains. Bessembinder's study of US stocks since 1926 found about 4% of companies made all the net gain above Treasury bills. A portfolio of 10 to 20 stocks can easily miss them. An index fund owns them automatically.
- Retail traders hurt themselves. Barber and Odean found the most active households earned about 11.4% a year against 17.9% for the market (1991 to 1996). The data is old, but the causes, overconfidence and panic, are still here.
- A 5% side portion limits the damage. If one pick falls to zero, you lose 5 points of your total. If one rises 10 times, you gain 45 points. That gain is rare.

## Main risks
- **Tax:** Selling index funds in a taxable account can trigger capital gains tax. In the US, long-term rates are 0%, 15% or 20%, plus possibly 3.8%. On $50,000 of gains at 15%, that is $7,500. Rules differ outside the US, and I do not know your country.
- **Concentration:** A small set of stocks can fall 50% or more. Check that your job, home and employer shares are not already a large part of your wealth.
- **Time:** Doing this properly may take roughly 5 to 7 hours a month. This figure is an estimate, not a measured one.
- **Costs outside the US:** Some countries charge extra on share purchases, such as UK stamp duty of 0.5%, which ETFs avoid. I am working from memory, so verify.
- **Luck versus skill:** A 12-month result tells you almost nothing.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You gave no reason for the switch. You have not said your amount, age, country, account type or experience. That suggests the idea comes from a feeling, not a plan. Most people who think they have an edge do not. Ask yourself whether you want better returns or just more control. Also check that you have an emergency fund and no high-interest debt first. Those matter more than any stock pick.

## Next steps
1. This week, write down your goal, your account type, and the tax cost of selling. Use new money, not sales, for any stock purchases.
2. Set a fixed dollar cap equal to 5% of your portfolio. Buy 5 to 8 stocks in stages over 3 months. Write down why you bought each one and what would make you sell.
3. Compare the stock slice with your index fund over identical dates each quarter. Make the real decision on 18 October 2031, not before. Stop sooner only if you break your written rules or cannot afford a loss.

## Board notes
- I overruled the Operator's 12-month stop rule. The Operator itself said 12 months is mostly noise, so I set 5 years.
- The Advocate's 15% limit was not supported. I chose 5% because the downside is small and no member justified more.
- Open point: the 2024 SPIVA small-cap figure ("30% trailed") looks odd and was not confirmed. I did not rely on it.

## Decision
Do not buy a £1,500 laptop now. Run a 30-day test on your current machine, then buy only if it clearly blocks you. Cap the spend at £900 unless you can name a specific task that needs more.

## Why
- Nobody on the board knows your current laptop, your project, or whether the £1,500 is spare cash. Those three facts decide this.
- A new laptop with 16GB RAM at £600 to £1,000 handles most side-project work, such as web, scripts, writing and light design. The extra £500 to £900 buys speed, not new ability.
- £1,500 is justified only for local AI, video, 3D, games or large builds. I do not know if you do any of these.
- The test costs £0. It turns a feeling into data.
- Waiting is cheap. Delay costs about 6 weeks on the old machine.

## Main risks
- **Money:** If the £1,500 comes from savings under three months of living costs, do not buy. Do not carry a credit card balance. Interest would wipe out any benefit.
- **Prices:** Reports say laptop prices rose in 2026 because of memory costs. The evidence is mostly non-UK and I could not verify UK figures. Black Friday (27 Nov 2026) discounts may be smaller than usual. Treat any saving as unproven.
- **Habit:** The likeliest failure is that you buy, the novelty fades in 4 to 8 weeks, and your evening time and energy stay the same.
- **Legal and tax:** UK online buyers generally get a 14-day cancellation right, and faulty goods can be rejected within 30 days. Credit card purchases over £100 may carry Section 75 protection. I am unsure of the details, so check gov.uk. If a project earns income, the UK £1,000 trading allowance may apply instead of expense claims. Check with HMRC or an accountant.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You asked whether to spend £1,500 but did not say what you are building or what is wrong with your current laptop. That is a warning sign. Buying a tool before naming the problem is a common way to feel productive without producing anything. Your record of finished projects tells you more than any spec sheet.

## Next steps
1. **From 19 Oct to 17 Nov:** Log each evening you work, the hours, and each time the laptop stopped you. Write down the task and the delay, for example "export takes 12 minutes".
2. **18 to 26 Nov:** If it blocked you in 3 or more sessions, check price history for 2 or 3 models at £700 to £900. Also check the maker's refurbished store.
3. **27 Nov:** Buy only if the log justifies it. Pay from spare cash. If you need more than £900, name the task first.

## Board notes
- I set the test at 30 days, not Operator's 2 weeks. Two weeks is about 14 hours of work, which is too thin for this decision.
- Operator's 3-blocks-per-week threshold and Skeptic's 5-minute build rule are arbitrary. I used the simpler count of blocked sessions. The right number is still open.
- Members disagreed on resale values (30 to 60%). None were sourced, so I gave them no weight.

## Decision
Do not buy a paid CRM yet. Run a 30 to 60 day pilot on HubSpot's free CRM with one event and one named owner. Commit money only if the pilot beats the spreadsheets on problems you can name and measure. Decide by mid-January 2027.

## Why
- You have not named the problem. A CRM fixes contact and follow-up pain. It does not fix logistics such as run-of-show, vendor budgets or seating. If most of your pain is logistics, HubSpot will disappoint.
- The pilot is cheap and reversible. The free tier costs $0 in licences. The real cost is staff time, which the board estimates at 40 to 80 hours in the first quarter. That figure is a guess.
- Price depends on the tier. Reported figures are about $900 to $1,200 a year for Starter (5 seats) and about $7,500 in year one for Professional Sales Hub with onboarding. These come from third-party blogs that disagree, so treat them as unconfirmed.
- Adoption is the most likely failure. Two systems running side by side is how this usually dies.

## Main risks
- **Money:** Paid tiers with automation add onboarding fees ($1,500 or more reported), annual commitments, and contact-based charges. Get a written quote for 5 seats.
- **Legal:** Attendee data falls under GDPR, CCPA or similar rules depending on where guests live. Check consent records and deletion process before importing. Confirm with a lawyer. I am not one.
- **Timing:** A rollout during a live event can cause a failure that costs more than the software. December holidays also slow the pilot.
- **Fit:** The free tier may lack the tasks or pipelines you need, which could make the trial fail for the wrong reason. Unverified.
- **Data:** Dirty spreadsheets give a dirty CRM. Budget 20 to 40 hours of cleanup.

## Honest criticism for the owner
You asked "should we move?" without saying what hurts. That is the weakest part of this question. Nobody on the board knows your event count, contact count, next event date, or whether you have lost sponsors or missed follow-ups. Without that, any answer is partly a guess. Also, "free" is not free. Your team's time is the main cost, and a tool will not fix a messy process.

## Next steps
1. This week: Write down 2 or 3 concrete problems and log lost hours for two weeks (15 minutes a day per person). Count missed follow-ups too. If the loss is small, fix the spreadsheets instead. The board did not agree on a hard hour threshold.
2. Weeks 3 to 4: Name one owner with about 5 hours a week. Import one past event into the free tier. Check that one person attending three events shows three records. Request a 5-seat written quote and one price check on an events-specific tool.
3. Pilot only if no major event falls in the window. Set a cutoff date after which old sponsor and contact sheets go read-only. Set a stop rule, for example under 80% of follow-ups logged by day 30.

## Board notes
- I overruled the Operator's fixed 8 hours a week rule. It is unsupported, and a missed sponsor renewal is a cost that hours do not capture. Use it as a rough guide only.
- I overruled the Advocate's "train everyone in a week" and "event registration" claims. Habit change takes 4 to 8 weeks, and HubSpot is not a full event platform.
- Open: whether an events-specific tool fits better than HubSpot. No one compared them.
